paper_design_summary: Four online experiments (total N = 1,814; Prolific and MTurk) randomly assigned participants to list which MLB or NFL teams would make that season's playoffs either using an LLM (Perplexity AI in Experiments 1 and 3, Google Bard in Experiments 2 and 4) or using their own judgment with an optional internet browser or search engine. Experiment 3 crossed LLM use with a 10-cent-per-correct-team incentive; Experiment 4 crossed LLM use in a first and a second listing stage. Outcomes are the number of unique teams listed (hypotheses, the preregistered primary outcome), the number and percentage of accurate teams judged against betting odds, self-reported confidence, calibration, and (in the SI) the number of unique teams listed by each condition's crowd.

eligibility.reason: All four experiments randomly assign people to an LLM (Perplexity AI or Google Bard) vs own judgment plus optional search (p. 4-5, p. 11-13), with 213 to 803 people analyzed per experiment. The doubt is scope: the task is listing which sports teams will make the playoffs, a finite set (30 MLB or 32 NFL teams) with correct answers judged against betting odds, and outputs are not judged on novelty, originality, or creativity. The outcomes are counts of hypotheses (fluency-like), counts and shares of accurate hypotheses, and a crowd-level count of unique teams (diversity-like, statistics only in the SI). If hypothesis generation counts as an ideation task, the study is core with a fluency outcome; if not, it is out of scope.

one_line_finding: Across four online experiments (N = 396, 213, 803, 400), people randomly assigned to an LLM listed more playoff-team hypotheses than people using their own judgment and search (Exp 1: 8.72 vs 5.99, d = 0.745, p. 5), with similar percent accuracy (p. 8), an effect matched by a 10-cent-per-correct-team incentive in Exp 3 (p. 6), and no crowd-level difference in unique teams (p. 11, SI Table S21).
open_questions: Is hypothesis generation over a finite answer set (which teams make the playoffs) a creative or ideation task under codebook section 1?
Arm-level and randomized counts, and the crowd-level unique-team statistics, are only in the SI Appendix (Tables S2, S21), which is not in this PDF.
In Experiment 4, the stage-1-only and stage-2-only LLM arms produce part of the total output without AI; ai_available_when_produced is coded mixed.
notes: Self-reported confidence (percent of own listed teams expected to be correct) and calibration (confidence minus accuracy) are in Fig. 4c-d and SI Table S5; LLM users were less confident and underconfident (p. 8-9). They are not listed as outcomes because they are self-reports. Experiment 3 also reports descriptive correlations between raw Perplexity output and participant lists (r = .334 for number, r = .795 for accuracy; 395 LLM-condition participants, 385 valid pastes; p. 10, Fig. 5). Benchmarking of LLM users at the 60th to 81st percentiles of no-LLM users is in SI Table S12 (p. 11). An ancillary occupation-guessing experiment is in SI Section 5, not in this PDF. The paper states the gain three ways: 36% more hypotheses on average (abstract, p. 2), 18% to 55% (significance statement, p. 2), and 30% to 58% (Summary of Findings, p. 4). No-LLM participants could optionally use a search engine, so the contrast is coded ai_vs_active; some may have used only their own judgment. arm_means_sds_ns not listed in statistics_available because arm ns are not printed (only means and SDs).
